identity.note: README names a Commodore 64 arcade port written with KickAssembler, CharPad and SpritePad. main.asm supplies a BASIC entry stub and directly configures VIC-II, interrupts, SID and memory banking. beam.asm implements capture, spinning, recapture and dual-fighter transitions; source modules cover formations, collision, waves, challenge stages, scores and disk persistence. identity.note: Joel Becker presents a 2018 game for the 1984 Macintosh 512K. The readable QuickBASIC listing contains an aiming/throwing game with cows, tornado attraction, a barn destination, ten levels, scoring, win/loss states, image DATA and sound routines.

classification.note: This is original homebrew source for a classic Macintosh, not reconstruction of a historical commercial game. The code uses native Macintosh QuickBASIC graphics/input primitives and is meant to be compiled as an application; Mini vMac is only a development/runtime option.

source_cpu.note: The original source was written specifically for Macintosh 512K. m68k is the platform-family inference from that unambiguous original machine, not evidence that the BASIC listing itself contains assembly or that any particular instruction minimum was audited.

target_cpu.note: The intended output is the native Macintosh application produced by Microsoft QuickBASIC 1.0 for Mac, with the author reporting an authentic Macintosh 512K test. No modern-host translation or PowerPC-native output is identified.

build.note: README names Microsoft QuickBASIC 1.0 for Macintosh. The source header explicitly says to compile the program to an application because interpreted execution is too slow. The tree consists of the main readable game listing and a separate music listing; the proprietary compiler is external and no scripted build is supplied. Limitations: The author-reported hardware test was not independently repeated. Compilation, launch, gameplay and byte equivalence remain unverified.

runtime_profiles.note: The author explicitly reports System 3.3 on a physical Macintosh 512K and Mini vMac. This is preserved as an author-tested configuration rather than a more general compatibility range or measured minimum.

ai.note: The README and the two BASIC listings contain no development-AI disclosure. Neither the 2018 date nor the game simulation establishes non-use.

relationships.note: The non-fork author repository is a single game with an accompanying music source. No explicit redistribution license appears in the complete three-file tree or inspected headers; public source availability is not described as open-source licensing. Current catalogue, source/decision registers and the all-prior review union were screened; no same-code-lineage record was found.

identity.note: BomberTalk is Matthew Deaves’s networked Bomberman clone and the reference game for his PeerTalk SDK. README, the native Toolbox entry point and bomb/explosion implementation establish an actual shared game core with classic Mac, Carbon and SDL backends.

classification.note: A new source-level Bomberman-style reimplementation with a portable C89 game core and platform backends. Classic Mac paths link the native Toolbox and networking libraries; no guest CPU interpreter or original game-ROM wrapper was found in the reviewed build/source paths.

source_cpu.note: The inspected sources identify Bomberman as design ancestry but do not analyze a specific historical binary or platform version. No historical source platform, CPU or machine-code input is asserted for this new implementation.

target_cpu.note: CMake explicitly selects Retro68 or RetroPPC. The Carbon build script requests ppc and i386 architecture slices. README additionally identifies a modern Apple-Silicon SDL build, supporting ARM64 as a directly described target; generic Linux wording does not establish every possible host architecture.

build.note: Classic builds require Retro68/RetroPPC plus clog and PeerTalk, fetched from floating main branches unless local checkouts are supplied. Carbon uses a legacy gcc/Apple SDK and defaults to OS X 10.4 despite README’s broader 10.3–10.7 claim. SDL has a separate build script described in README. The latest asset pipeline still needs a hardware or genuine-QuickDraw check for its SE sprite tier. Limitations: Author-reported prior cross-hardware rounds do not verify the exact current snapshot. No dependency resolution, build, network session, launch or gameplay test was performed.

runtime_profiles.note: The documented minimum is Mac SE with 8 MHz 68000, 4 MB RAM, System 6.0.8 and MacTCP. Other README examples include Performa 6200/6400 and modern hosts, but no comparable universal minimum is established for those outputs. The current SE sprite-format validation caveat is retained separately from earlier game tests.

ai.note: Explicit code-commit co-author trailers name Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context); for example b576eafdcb1610297db089981cf448dab12593a6 changes network/lobby code. This supports AI usage and the tool label Claude. The model/context label is preserved here, not turned into extra tool names. CLAUDE.md alone would not establish usage.

relationships.note: PeerTalk and clog are external dependencies, while the classic, Carbon and SDL versions remain one BomberTalk project. No root LICENSE is present in the complete pinned tree, so an open-source redistribution grant is not assumed. The tree also includes third-party reference books and generated assets whose rights were not audited. Current catalogue, source/decision registers and the all-prior review union were screened; no same-code-lineage record was found.

identity.note: A Macintosh Classic adaptation of the PICO-8 Celeste Classic by Maddy Thorson and Noel Berry. It vendors lemon32767/ccleste’s hand-translated game logic, adds Macintosh Toolbox entry/audio/input/display code and reuses infrastructure from the author’s Just One Boss port.

classification.note: A native source translation/port, not a CPU-emulation wrapper. The game’s Lua logic was translated into C by ccleste; this build compiles celeste.c as C++ for a 16.16 fixed-point type and substitutes a PICO-8 drawing API over a native Mac framebuffer.

source_cpu.note: The original is a Lua PICO-8 cartridge with a virtual API, passed through ccleste’s portable C translation. No physical source CPU is established or needed; no x86 or ARM architecture is inferred from PICO-8’s development host.

target_cpu.note: README and mac_main.c explicitly target a 68000 classic Macintosh; build.sh selects m68k-apple-macos/retro68.toolchain.cmake. CMake’s fixed-point C++ compilation and no-exception/no-RTTI flags support native 68k output without requiring an FPU.

build.note: CMake defines Celeste, a phase-diagnostic build and a no-music diagnostic build. build.sh requires an external Retro68 installation and Ninja; generated sprite/map/sound/music C inputs are included. Documentation reports 30 FPS in Mini vMac but later records 2–3 FPS on actual 4 MB Classic hardware, so that emulator result is not generalized to real hardware. Limitations: No independent build, emulator session, real-hardware session, gameplay or byte comparison was performed. The latest performance-plan text is not evidence that its proposed optimization was completed.

runtime_profiles.note: The original target is 68000/System 6 or 7. Full audio raises the author’s stated requirement to at least 2 MB; 1 MB systems need a reduced build. The approximately 1.6 MB image exceeds an ordinary 800 KB floppy and notes recommend SD-backed storage. The real 4 MB Classic report remains 2–3 FPS.

ai.note: The inspected README, build files, porting notes and selected game/Toolbox sources do not explicitly disclose AI development. Reusing infrastructure from an AI-disclosed sibling and prose style do not establish AI usage in this distinct repository.

relationships.note: The source lineage is original PICO-8 Celeste Classic to ccleste to this Mac port, with a shared shell from Just One Boss. Rights are a material caveat: PORTING-NOTES calls this a private hobby port and says to ask both original and ccleste authors before distribution; README’s freely distributed game description is not a license grant. No root license is present. Current catalogue and prior-family screening found no already-indexed ccleste/Mac-port code lineage.

identity.note: Mitchell Vizensky’s native C port of Ayla Nonsense’s PICO-8 Just One Boss. README explicitly reports creator permission. The game/entities sources contain boss stages, reflection timelines, attack patterns, high scores and victory flow, beyond an initial scaffold.

classification.note: A Lua-to-C source translation with a small PICO-8 API compatibility layer, native entity/timeline logic, generated cartridge data and Macintosh Toolbox presentation. The API layer emulates drawing semantics, not a guest processor instruction stream.

source_cpu.note: The source is a Lua PICO-8 game and associated cartridge data; PORTING-PLAN explicitly labels its CPU virtualized. No physical source ISA is inferred.

target_cpu.note: README explicitly targets a System 6/7, 8 MHz 68000 Macintosh Classic. build.sh selects the m68k-apple-macos Retro68 toolchain, and CMake links native C game and Mac platform sources into an APPL output.

build.note: Retro68 and Ninja are required externally. CMake links checked-in generated data, native platform code, engine and entities; it uses software libm rather than requiring an FPU. README says most verification used a modern-host real-logic harness. PORTING-PLAN and leading source comments preserve older incomplete-phase descriptions, so current implemented routines were checked instead of accepting every milestone as synchronized. Limitations: No compilation, host harness, emulator, real hardware or gameplay was run in this review; neither completeness nor actual 68000 frame rate is independently verified.

runtime_profiles.note: System 6/7 on an 8 MHz 68000 monochrome Macintosh Classic is explicitly targeted. Build notes describe emulator and real-hardware transfer routes, but do not provide an independently verified minimum RAM or acceptable frame-rate result.

ai.note: README explicitly states that the port was developed with Claude Code, supporting ai.usage=true and the named tool. This is direct author attribution rather than an inference from an instruction file.

relationships.note: README links Ayla Nonsense’s original cartridge repository and explicitly says the port has creator permission. Original game design/art/music remain Ayla’s, the port code is attributed to Mitchell Vizensky, and the PICO-8 font is CC0. No broad source redistribution license is supplied; permission to port is not silently promoted to an OSI license. The related Celeste port shares infrastructure but is a different game.

identity.note: Semantle Plus is a native Macintosh Plus word-neighborhood game. main.c implements the Mac interface and game rounds; similarity.c implements indexed lookup, quantized vector scoring, top-50 rankings and deterministic out-of-vocabulary fallback.

classification.note: A source-level word-game implementation with a native Toolbox application. word2vec training and quantization occur offline; the Mac executes integer similarity logic and checked-in data. The host-only CMake executable is a test harness, not the target game and not a classic-Mac CPU emulator.

source_cpu.note: No historical binary or original machine-language game is analyzed by the inspected repository. Its inputs are a word2vec model and text corpus, so no historical source CPU or platform is assigned from the modern training host.

target_cpu.note: build.sh and README select the Retro68 m68k-apple-macos toolchain; CMake builds APPL/MacBinary output for Retro68 and explicitly comments on keeping the application suitable for a stock Macintosh Plus. The generic host test executable does not justify additional target-CPU entries.

build.note: The classic build compiles main.c and similarity.c with a pre-generated model_data.h, requests one classic code segment and produces MacBinary/disk-image outputs. Regeneration requires external tmikolov/word2vec, text8, a host compiler and Python; these are not needed merely to use checked-in model data. CMake’s host test target validates the similarity engine only. Limitations: No model training, compilation, tests, emulator launch or gameplay was performed; all build/runtime verification flags remain null.

runtime_profiles.note: The documented target is Macintosh Plus running System 3. README and source deliberately use GetNextEvent/SystemTask rather than WaitNextEvent. App size and a 1 MB application budget are not asserted as a proven total-machine RAM minimum; CD-ROM packaging additionally needs appropriate SCSI hardware/driver.

ai.note: The inspected files explain word2vec as game data/training technology, not AI-assisted software development. No coding-assistant disclosure was found in the README, build or selected source; ai.usage remains unknown rather than true merely because the game uses word embeddings.

relationships.note: The native game is distinct from its external word2vec trainer, text8 corpus and host-test executable. No root license exists in the complete pinned tree, and no broader rights grant for code, corpus or generated embeddings is established. The Semantle-style gameplay label is not used to assert source ancestry from an uninspected upstream game. Current catalogue and the full prior-review root union contain no matching game lineage.

identity.note: Preserves and reconstructs Chuck Shotton/BIAP Systems’ 1989 Beast 1.0. The game’s CODE resources, Pascal routines and Swift board logic are present, with movement, block pushing, enemy pursuit, win/loss and settings.

classification.note: Annotated 68000 disassembly was lifted into Pascal and translated routine by routine into Swift. The AppKit shell calls native game logic; its PICT interpreter decodes graphics commands, not CPU instructions or Macintosh hardware. Treat as binary-derived reconstruction and native port, not original-author source.

source_cpu.note: The CODE 2 listing contains Motorola address/data registers, 68000 opcodes and Macintosh A-line Toolbox traps. Reconstructed Pascal preserves CODE offsets and A5 globals. This establishes m68k input independently of a generic classic-Mac label.

target_cpu.note: build-app.sh explicitly requests arm64 and x86_64 Swift builds. These are native modern Mac outputs; retained 68000 disassembly is an input artifact and does not imply a rebuilt classic-Mac target.

build.note: SwiftPM defines BeastCore, the AppKit executable and a test target; the shell script packages resources and applies an ad-hoc signature. Original resource data and generated artwork are included. No Pascal rebuild recipe or complete-game equivalence test was established. Limitations: No game was compiled, launched, played, hardware-tested or byte-compared. All independent verification flags remain unknown.

runtime_profiles.note: Package.swift declares macOS 14 and Swift tools 5.9. The native shell uses a 60 Hz timer and original-sized board coordinates. QDRandom explicitly has not been checked against a real ROM; documentation lists deliberate menu, storage, input, zoom and safety changes. No precise historic OS/RAM minimum is claimed.

ai.note: Actual implementation commit 8729de48 adds the Swift game, shell and build files and includes an explicit Claude coauthor trailer. Its model label is recorded only as an upstream attribution, not independent model-version verification. Nine available commit messages were inspected.

relationships.note: One reconstruction lineage covers its disassembly, Pascal and Swift stages. No matching Beast lineage appears in the catalogue or prior-review union. The Swift port is MIT licensed, except original-derived Artwork.swift and AppIcon.icns; the original application, disassembly and art retain Chuck Shotton/BIAP rights.

identity.note: Reconstructs the Bunnells’ Megaroids from a historical book listing, corrected OCR and binary-extracted sprite data, then implements a modern Swift game. The README gives both 1984 and 1985 original dates; no exact original release date is selected here.

classification.note: Source-led recovery and translation rather than a general emulator. The recovered C contains Toolbox calls and hardware-oriented code; Swift GameEngine, Ship and SoundEngine implement game-state progression, motion and audio directly. Recovered Megaroids.c is an assembled reference, not an untouched original archive.

source_cpu.note: The preserved C includes a 68000 compiler string, inline 68k operations, low-memory globals and original Macintosh framebuffer addresses. These establish the m68k Macintosh implementation, separate from the Swift host architecture.

target_cpu.note: The Xcode project builds a macOS Swift application but does not pin an explicit output ISA in the inspected settings. Do not infer Apple silicon or Intel support from modern macOS alone; target_cpu is intentionally empty.

build.note: An Xcode project and source/assets are present. A git-ignored project.xcconfig is a required base configuration and contains user-supplied signing/bundle settings; it must be supplied locally. The README’s Xcode 16+ heading conflicts with its later 26.4.1+ instruction. No exact compiler minimum is asserted. Limitations: No game was compiled, launched, played, hardware-tested or byte-compared. All independent verification flags remain unknown.

runtime_profiles.note: Application target deployment settings are macOS 26.0, overriding project-level 26.4 settings. The source runs a 60 Hz timer and original-resolution game model. It deliberately changes audio mixing, hyperspace behavior, friction and presentation, so advertised pixel fidelity is not treated as verified equivalence.

ai.note: README explicitly credits Claude Code for the Swift implementation and overall porting approach. That direct development disclosure supports AI usage; the .claude ignore entry is not used as evidence. Both available commit messages were also inspected.

relationships.note: Recovered C and Swift are one project lineage, with no Megaroids project found in the current catalogue/prior union. This does not duplicate other independent Asteroids-like games. No repository-wide license was found in the complete tree; the author reserves original game rights to the Bunnell family, so availability is not a blanket reuse grant.

identity.note: Robert Munafo publishes his June 1984 Macintosh Missile Command implementation, with later revisions.

classification.note: Original-author Pascal preservation: missile movement, fireballs, rounds, scoring and Toolbox UI are implemented.

source_cpu.note: Author identifies the original 128K Macintosh; m68k is inferred from that explicit machine target.

target_cpu.note: Historical Macintosh output remains m68k. Later PowerPC compatibility claims do not establish native PowerPC recompilation.

build.note: Lisa Pascal source and resource definitions are published. Historical interface units and resource compilation remain required. Limitations: No game was compiled, launched, played, hardware-tested or byte-compared. All independent verification flags remain unknown.

relationships.note: Independent Macintosh implementation, distinct from indexed Atari arcade disassembly. Source-specific GPL-2.0 notice applies; generic website footer licensing is separate.

identity.note: The maintainer’s Multi Pong is a native multi-window Pong variant developed in a 68k Macintosh programming study group. The reviewed implementation contains moving balls, an opponent paddle, collision against visible regions of draggable windows, five difficulty choices, scoring and an end condition at seven points.

classification.note: Original source-level homebrew in C using Macintosh Toolbox windows, QuickDraw regions, menus and event handling. The user changes the playfield through actual Mac windows; this is an implemented game rather than a generic window shell. The linked browser edition is a delivery option, not evidence of a separate browser reimplementation.

source_cpu.note: No historical binary, machine-code input or recovered original Pong source is identified. This is new homebrew and does not establish a historical source CPU or source platform; those arrays are empty.

target_cpu.note: README situates development specifically in the 68k Macintosh programming group and instructs building with THINK C 6.0; the source uses direct classic Toolbox/QuickDraw calls. Together these establish the intended m68k output. The generic Performa reference is not treated as proof of native PowerPC code generation.

ai.note: The inspected README and complete available 13-commit message history contain no explicit development-AI disclosure or assistant co-author trailer. This does not establish non-use; age, coding style and filenames are not AI evidence.

identity.note: Unofficial native recompilation of Macintosh Battle Chess. docs/DATA.md identifies the exact recovery baseline as MacPlay Battle Chess 1.0.2, with an embedded 1988–93 Interplay notice; the general 1991 release label does not date that exact binary. Reviewed code includes legal moves, piece lists, saves, animation sequencing, game sessions and native UI.

classification.note: Binary-derived recovery into a C11 engine and C++17/SDL3 host, explicitly not a clean-room project. recovered_core.c translates original file-offset routines into host-valued structs rather than a mapped 68k memory image; animation.c retains original routine provenance beside native helpers, while QuickDrawControl.cpp recreates controls through SDL. No guest-CPU interpreter is in these inspected game/host paths.

build.note: CMake 3.20 and C11/C++17 build a source-only core by default; the application additionally needs SDL3 3.4 and a matching external prepared data pack. CMake checks for generated catalogs, animation pixels, a 32,000-byte opening book and assets. The repository intentionally omits original resources and the extraction scripts needed to create the pack. Upstream dated test and playability claims are reported separately from verification here. Limitations: No dependency installation, game compilation, tests, launch, gameplay, hardware check or binary comparison was performed. All build-verification flags remain null. Original idle-animation triggering, timing/audio, computer choices, save exchange and modem interoperability remain incomplete or unverified upstream.

runtime_profiles.note: The application needs a desktop video/audio environment supported by SDL3 and the matching external data pack. No exact minimum CPU, RAM, macOS version or Linux distribution is established. Original Macintosh source architecture and dummy-driver smoke tests are not host runtime minima.

ai.note: The inspected README and complete available 11-commit message history contain no explicit development-AI disclosure or assistant co-author trailer. This does not establish non-use; age, coding style and filenames are not AI evidence. MIT covers contributions only to the extent contributors can license them; NOTICE excludes original code/data, Apple fonts and other third-party material. Screenshots contain original artwork, while required data and the separate recovery workspace are not distributed. identity.note: The maintainer identifies this as HTML5 3Tris and explicitly links its original Macintosh 68K predecessor. The implemented JavaScript game includes a 3D block grid, eight shape types, timed descent, rotations, placement collision, filled-plane clearing, score/level progression and game over, with separate device-oriented pages.

classification.note: A browser JavaScript recreation with its own Canvas/3D rendering and input code. The inspected gameplay uses direct grid and shape logic, not emulation of Macintosh CPU or Toolbox calls. No binary-derived recovery method or original source translation is asserted.

source_cpu.note: README explicitly calls the predecessor a Macintosh 68K game, establishing m68k historical ancestry. No original binary was inspected and no more precise 680x0 minimum or PowerPC edition is inferred. The README’s broad decade wording is not used as an exact release date.

target_cpu.note: The output is HTML5/JavaScript executed by a browser. The inspected pages load local scripts and media; they do not establish a native output ISA. The historical m68k ancestry is not copied into target_cpu.

README explicitly notes an unresolved polygon-distance visualization bug and says Android was untested. The current behavior of obsolete app-cache/browser paths has not been checked. Limitations: No dependency installation, game compilation, tests, launch, gameplay, hardware check or binary comparison was performed. All build-verification flags remain null.

No matching root or 3Tris lineage was found in the current catalogue/prior-review union. identity.note: Preservation mirror of the original Macintosh Wolfenstein 3D First/Second Encounter source release, attributed in the preserved release note to Bill Heineman and Chris DeSalvo. The note dates the Macintosh commercial release to October 1994 and the source-release account to January 2000; the GitHub root itself is a later third-party archive. WolfMain.c implements the level/game loop, player/enemy/projectile movement and game progression.

classification.note: Historical original-source preservation with native Macintosh Toolbox support, C gameplay and separate 68k/PPC assembly renderers. The preserved note says this Mac version descends from the SNES adaptation and uses BSP rendering, so it is not collapsed into the tracker’s DOS-derived Wolf ports merely by title. No new decompilation is claimed.

source_cpu.note: The release note explicitly distinguishes Macintosh 68000 and PowerPC editions. Wolf.68k contains D/A registers, MOVEM/MOVE/ADDX/DBF instructions, and Wolf.ppc contains PowerPC register, TOC and code-section conventions. These independently establish both source families; the SNES ancestry does not become a claimed source binary platform for this Mac archive.

target_cpu.note: The archive retains distinct native 68k and PowerPC renderer paths and a CodeWarrior project. Both architectures describe preserved original outputs, not modern host targets or verified successful rebuilds. README’s historical runtime-generated-scaler description is not copied as current behavior: Wolf.68k explicitly records a revision to tight loops, and current SetupScalers68k.c builds a reciprocal table with a disabled older ScaleGlue call path.

build.note: The source-release note says the project was updated from CodeWarrior DR/4 to Pro 5. The tree contains Wolf3D.mcp, assembly/object artifacts and separate proprietary music libraries, but no complete game resource/asset pack or reproducible modern recipe. Source still uses resource IDs and GetResource/LoadAResource calls. Project-file strings name both MacOS 68K/PPC linkers and legacy libraries; they do not prove all dependencies are present. Limitations: No dependency installation, game compilation, tests, launch, gameplay, hardware check or binary comparison was performed. All build-verification flags remain null. README’s original author build claim is historical and does not verify this mirror.

runtime_profiles.note: Mac.c’s 68k initialization explicitly rejects systems before 6.0.7, requires 32-bit Color QuickDraw, and selects an 8-bit monitor at least 512×384. Its 68000/68020/68030 cases display speed warnings rather than a reliable universal minimum-CPU rule. The PowerPC branch skips the OS gate with a 7.1 comment; no independently established PPC minimum or numeric RAM requirement is asserted.

ai.note: The inspected README and complete available 1-commit message history contain no explicit development-AI disclosure or assistant co-author trailer. This does not establish non-use; age, coding style and filenames are not AI evidence.

relationships.note: One archived mirror of the original Mac source lineage, counted once. Existing records were compared without re-researching their roots: earok/AkikoWolf credits AWolf/PSP/id DOS source, agranlund/wolf derives from Wolf4SDL/id, and kweepa/wolf64 is a C64 assembly raycaster. In contrast, this preserved author note explicitly identifies a SNES-derived implementation rather than the PC version, with BSP visibility; RefBsp.c and separate Mac renderer paths corroborate material implementation differences, not merely a new target platform. No matching Blzut3/Heineman/Burger Mac source root appears in the complete prior-review union. No general root license is supplied; the release note expressly reserves Steve Hales/Jim Nitchals music-driver rights and requires separate permission for reuse. Public source availability is not treated as an unrestricted redistribution grant.

identity.note: The author identifies Sparks as the beginnings of a Macintosh game written around 2000 and this repository as an attempt to get its original classic Macintosh code running. The pinned tree contains the game loop, entity, player, star-field, renderer and resource source, rather than only an announcement.

classification.note: Original-source restoration of an unfinished game prototype. Main.cpp initializes the classic Toolbox and drives Game_RunFrame; this is neither a binary decompilation nor a modern independent remake. The README explicitly declines to characterize the historical work as a finished game.

source_cpu.note: The preserved original Macintosh C++ tree has separate 68K object rules, CPlusOptions-68K with the near model, 68K runtime libraries and a Sparks.68k link target. Together with the author’s original-code statement, this directly establishes m68k source provenance rather than inferring it from the approximate date.

target_cpu.note: The MPW makefile explicitly targets both Sparks.68k through ILink and Sparks.ppc through PPCLink. These are documented build targets; successful output was not established.

build.note: Inspected the MPW makefile, classic Toolbox bootstrap and complete tree inventory. The build requires the historical CPlus/PPCCPlus, ILink/PPCLink and Rez tools and classic Macintosh libraries; Resources.r and Resources.rsrc are present. No root license grant was found in the tree or README. The project remains explicitly unfinished. Limitations: No compilation, tests, execution, gameplay or binary comparison was performed. All build booleans remain null.

runtime_profiles.note: Main.cpp tests Color QuickDraw availability and an 8-bit display mode, then allocates a GWorld backbuffer. These are implementation requirements, but the inspected material supplies no authoritative minimum CPU model or RAM for a usable game; no runnable hardware profile is asserted.

ai.note: The inspected README and original-code/bootstrap material contain no explicit development-AI disclosure. This is a bounded negative search, not evidence of non-use; usage remains unknown.

relationships.note: The README mentions another copy in /game/space without identifying a repository. This record covers the author’s Sparks restoration root once; that undeclared copy is not promoted separately. The root was absent from the current catalogue and prior-review/source/decision root index. Limitations: The other copy’s provenance and current location remain unresolved.

identity.note: README identifies an open-source recreation/extension of Cary Torkelson’s Mac shareware game, with explicit instructions for playing the original. The repository preserves reference screenshots and original help alongside a separate MiniScript implementation.

build.note: Assembly source, included ZX0 routine and a runner executable are present. The source uses Amiga include files and an NC: include path, so the complete assembler environment remains untested. No independent assembly, execution or byte-match check was performed.

These conditions are described without manufacturing a numeric minimum profile.

identity.note: The root README describes the author's reusable C64 tools and routines. Inspected source spans a VIC-II raster-test suite, native Koala graphics viewer, SID metadata/player inspection and a CBM2040 disk-file copier. The root is retained as one development/analysis collection rather than splitting each routine into a project.

classification.note: The collection supplies actual native raster/video tests and graphics routines plus host-side analysis/recovery scripts. sid_info.py parses SID headers and recognizes SidTracker64 player instruction/variable layout; cbm2040_to_d64.py uses cbmctrl/cbmread/c1541 to copy legacy disk files into D64/D71 images. This is development and analysis tooling, not reconstruction of a complete historical game.

source_cpu.note: The SID player analyzer explicitly describes and inspects JMP, LDX, JSR, LDA and STA sequences and little-endian instruction operands in a C64 SidTracker64 music payload. This supports a 6502-family analysis input; the disk and graphics data themselves are CPU-independent.

target_cpu.note: test_double_irq.asm explicitly names target Commodore 64 (MOS 6510 / 6569 PAL-B) and implements processor-port banking, raster interrupts and native 6502 instructions. The suite Makefile assembles PRGs with 64tass and selects the PAL C64/VIC-II 6569 model for x64sc.

build.note: Root README names cc65 for the older routines; the VIC-II Makefile has 13 concrete 64tass PRG targets and a header/symbol-presence integrity check. Source and build recipes were inspected but not executed. Limitations: The test README retains stale eight-test claims/sample results while the current Makefile names 13 targets. Its production-grade/cycle-exact wording was not independently validated, so no blanket build or runtime success is asserted.

runtime_profiles.note: The inspected VIC-II sources document PAL/63-cycle timing and give a VICE launch command, but the collection mixes test programs, older routines and host Python tools. No verified minimum-hardware profile covering a named successfully reproduced output was established. Limitations: Do not infer collection-wide NTSC compatibility or RAM requirements from the platform. No emulator or physical hardware testing occurred.

ai.note: Root/tree inventory, selected assembly/Python/documentation files and latest ten commit messages were inspected. None explicitly attributes development to a named generative-AI tool; usage remains unknown. Limitations: Writing style and project references do not establish AI usage.

relationships.note: The VIC-II README states that these tests support emulation accuracy and disassembly-pattern analysis for the already tracked Regenerator 2000. The repository also contains older independent reusable routines and recovery scripts; it is a separate supporting toolkit, not a mirror of that disassembler or of the author's tracked game disassemblies.

identity.note: The root hardware project includes creator-attributed C64 game-control modifications and an editable Joystick5plus1Test.c tester. Its Impossible Mission 3 component includes instructions, a Python patcher and a 170-byte native payload. This record covers the coherent software companion and authored patch work, not bare PCB fabrication files.

classification.note: Native C64 control patches and a development tester. The Impossible Mission 3 patcher checks input/payload CRC32 values, verifies three expected byte sequences, writes jump replacements and injects the payload. The root README separately attributes Commando, Wizball, Turrican and other patches to this author. No complete disassembly or source reconstruction is claimed.

source_cpu.note: The targeted C64 image patches use 6502 instructions: patch.py replaces 20 50 FD (JSR $FD50) with 4C 50 81 (JMP $8150), and other hooks use 4C and EA (JMP/NOP). The payload was statically inspected as bytes and begins 20 50 FD A2 99 BD 61 81 9D 3F 03 CA D0 F7, consistent with native 6502 code. A specific silicon revision is not inferred.

target_cpu.note: The injected payload and replacement hook bytes are native 6502 instructions for the original C64 game image, rather than a host CPU emulator. The Python patcher and C tester do not establish any additional host CPU target.

build.note: The root distributes patched PRG/CRT/D64 artifacts and tester source/binary. Impossible Mission 3 instructions run VICE cartconv, python patch.py, then cartconv again against the user's own game image. Source and payload were inspected without compiling the tester, executing the patcher or playing patched binaries. Limitations: All build flags stay unknown. The payload is binary machine code rather than editable assembly source. Compatible input has CRC32 0x19176BAB; successful patching would intentionally change bytes, not establish original-byte identity.

runtime_profiles.note: The documentation specifies C64 joystick-button behavior and warns that replacement SID devices with incompatible POTX/POTY behavior can cause unwanted jumping. It does not establish a tested minimum CPU/RAM or complete hardware-compatibility profile. Limitations: C64/VIC20/Amiga are mentioned for the physical joystick; that does not establish VIC20 or Amiga software targets for the inspected C64 patches.

ai.note: Root/tree inventory, selected READMEs, C tester and Python patcher plus latest ten commit messages contain no explicit generative-AI attribution. Usage remains unknown. Limitations: Bounded inspection, not proof of non-use.

relationships.note: ricardoquesada/c64-games-unijoysticle links this repository as one source of its mixed patch collection. Here the creator specifically identifies his own modifications and supplies a concrete guarded patcher, so this is distinct authored software work; the downstream aggregation is not promoted. The nested Impossible Mission 3 patch remains evidence for this root control-modification project rather than a second record.

identity.note: The repository describes an Amiga demo disassembly and preserves a packed THE_OUTSIDER artifact, IRA configuration and generated listing, plus a dec/ directory containing an unpacked binary, configuration and listing. This is one coherent research project at the repository root.

The inspected IRA configurations select small code spans, while much of the generated material remains data directives. Classify this as an initial partial disassembly, without claiming a fully annotated or rebuilt demo.

source_cpu.note: Both IRA configuration files explicitly select MACHINE 68000, supported by the inspected Motorola data/address-register instructions and Amiga custom-register addresses.

target_cpu.note: The generated reconstruction is 68000 assembly with 68000-configured analysis and reassembled artifacts. This establishes the output architecture, not a minimum runnable machine.

build.note: The root listing gives THE_OUTSIDER and THE_OUTSIDER.reassembled the same Git blob SHA, b8b582cb06810f5cb428845bb42a45e8198e48bd, and the same 84224-byte size. This establishes equality of the stored artifacts, but no independent assembly, original-release provenance check or execution was performed; build and byte-exact flags remain unknown. Limitations: A stored file labelled reassembled is not evidence of a reproducible rebuild. No build recipe was found in the complete tree.

runtime_profiles.note: The one-line README, configurations, inspected listings and repository tree establish no explicit RAM, chipset, OS or minimum runnable CPU requirements.

ai.note: The complete tree, one available commit message, README and selected listings contain no explicit development-AI disclosure. IRA is an identified disassembler, not evidence of generative AI use.

relationships.note: The assembly headers credit IRA V2.12 and its authors. The unpacked material is part of the same demo investigation and is not a second project. No project licence or original demo author attribution was established in the inspected files.

identity.note: Torsten Curdt publishes his own rotating-ellipses and cube-in-a-mirror parts from The Electronic Knights' 1994 Rampage trackmo. Both source headers credit Curdt/TEK and 1993 development. The archive also includes sprite data, per-part include files, screenshots and a disk image; it does not claim to preserve every demo part.

source_cpu.note: The original sources use Motorola 68k data/address registers, MOVEM, DBF, RTE and Amiga custom-chip addresses. The inspected files do not select an exact processor variant, so retain the broad m68k architecture rather than asserting a minimum 68000.

target_cpu.note: The preserved output remains native m68k assembly for Amiga custom hardware; no translated host implementation is present.

build.note: The complete tree contains no common makefile or build instructions. mirror.s includes setup.i, which is absent from that tree, and the source retains historical assembler directives and fixed test addresses. The supplied disk image does not prove these published sources currently rebuild, so all build flags remain unknown. Limitations: No compilation, execution or byte comparison was performed; the missing setup.i is a concrete reproducibility gap.

runtime_profiles.note: The author README and selected code do not state a reliable minimum CPU, RAM, chipset or OS configuration. Fixed source addresses and the existence of an ADF are not used to infer runtime requirements.

ai.note: README, source headers, complete tree and all four returned commits disclose no development-AI use. Historical source dates do not establish non-use in every later maintenance action.

relationships.note: The README explicitly identifies Curdt's contribution to TEK's Rampage and releases his sources under the Apache licence. Embedded manager code credits Captain Bifat/TEK; the archive's own authorship statement is not a new ownership claim over every third-party contribution or the full disk image.

identity.note: Jonathan Bennett/Antiriad publishes Planet Jazz's Planet Disco Balls, a 64 KB intro released at Revision 2021, together with its original source, asset-conversion/build environment and shared demo framework.

It is neither a disassembly nor a CPU-emulation wrapper; the complete repository is the appropriate coherent scope.

His Projects source is MIT-licensed; bundled tools and emulator retain their separate licences. This is a distinct intro from the already tracked Parcade by the same author.

identity.note: Greaseweazle Rescue is a substantive AutoIt Windows GUI and recovery-workflow layer over Greaseweazle. The current root contains v1.3.4 source and release notes, despite root README installation examples still naming v1.3.1. It handles PC/DOS/VGACopy, AmigaDOS ADF and C64/1541 D64 workflows.

classification.note: The source implements format detection, SCP capture, standard ADF/D64 conversion, direct retry reads, reports, hashes and conflict-safe publication of complete logical images. Its DOS path additionally implements targeted head-by-head adaptive rereads and multi-SCP sector merging. This is independent recovery automation around an existing decoder, rather than a claim to have reimplemented Greaseweazle's flux codecs. Limitations: The multi-SCP handler explicitly rejects Amiga and C64 modes. Advanced adaptive two-pass sector recovery is DOS-only; Amiga/C64 use direct Greaseweazle retry reads. Complete ADF/D64 standard sectors do not preserve all copy-protection or unusual flux data, so SCP remains the archival master.

source_cpu.note: This tool reads floppy flux and disk-image sector data rather than reconstructing any original executable CPU instruction set. Supported disk platforms do not establish source CPUs.

target_cpu.note: The AutoIt source, README and v1.3.4 release establish Windows as host, but no explicit x86/x64 target selection or minimum processor architecture was found. No architecture is inferred from AutoIt or Windows.

build.note: The repository supplies a substantial AutoIt source script and tagged v1.3.4 release, whose inspected release assets list is empty. Root README describes a compiled EXE but no such artifact was verified. No AutoIt compilation, hardware capture, recovery trial or independent image comparison was performed; all build flags remain unknown. Limitations: The 100_PERCENT_OK label means all expected standard sectors were reported present; it is not historical binary equivalence or completeness of copy-protected flux.

runtime_profiles.note: The creator README explicitly requires Windows 7 or later, Greaseweazle gw.exe and compatible hardware/drive for physical capture. Record the documented OS requirement, leaving CPU/RAM unclaimed.

ai.note: Inspected README, complete current root, source and both available commit messages include no explicit AI development attribution. The README's self-evaluation tone is not evidence of AI authorship.

relationships.note: The README explicitly credits and requires Keir Fraser's already-tracked Greaseweazle tools. This separate AutoIt implementation adds workflow, reporting and DOS-sector rescue logic and is not a mirrored copy of those tools. The root license is MIT.

identity.note: sark02 identifies this as an Atari ST/STE/Falcon port of Williams Defender; the repository contains gameplay C, 68k platform assembly, asset-generation tools, build instructions and a player manual as one coherent project.

classification.note: Original arcade gameplay functions were translated from published 6809 assembly into C, with some visual algorithms recreated from observation. This is a native original-source-derived port; it is not labelled a binary-derived reconstruction or RE-derived port.

source_cpu.note: README explicitly identifies the source gameplay as published Williams Defender 6809 assembly and distinguishes the arcade main processor from its separate sound board. The source architecture records only the demonstrated 6809 gameplay source.

target_cpu.note: Makefile compiles both C and assembly using -DM68000 and -m68000. This establishes the native output architecture independently of the original arcade 6809 source.

build.note: BUILD reports an actual Ubuntu 22.04/WSL build using m68k-elf GCC 14.2.0 and describes defender.st and defender.zip outputs. README documents supported machines and credits community playtesters; HOWTO explains playable controls and configuration. These support author-reported compilable, runnable and playable values. Limitations: No independent build, execution or binary comparison was performed. Byte-exactness remains unknown; original-source translation is not a binary match claim.

ai.note: The inspected README production-tool list, BUILD, Makefile and player manual do not disclose AI use. That absence is not evidence of non-use.

relationships.note: README credits the published historicalsource/defender arcade source as the gameplay lineage, liblzg for compression and Hatari-derived YM2149 sample-volume data. The independently implemented Atari graphics, sound and I/O make this a distinct port rather than an archive mirror.

identity.note: Diego Parrilla identifies the preserved material as his own 1989 Atari ST intro/cracktro and Ghostbusters-themed sampling demo, written under the name Canal 23. The repository holds both assembly sources, resources and shared modern build setup, so it is one source-restoration record at the repository root.

source_cpu.note: README names the author's 68000 programming work; GHOST.S contains Motorola data/address registers, MOVEM, DBF, GEMDOS/XBIOS traps and direct Atari PSG access. The preserved original source is 68000 assembly.

target_cpu.note: Both Makefile_intro and Makefile_sampling explicitly pass -m68000 to VASM and link an Atari TOS/PRG output via the m68k-atari-mint toolchain.

build.note: README reports that the author rebuilt the old code with VASM and links a Hatari recording, supporting an author-reported runnable demo. Current compilability remains unknown: the checked tree contains src/INTRO.S and src/GHOST.S, but the makefiles request src/intro.s and src/ghost.s, which differ on case-sensitive filesystems. Limitations: No build or execution was performed. A historical successful rebuild does not resolve the current source-path case mismatch. Playability is inapplicable to these demos and remains null; no byte comparison is reported.

ai.note: The inspected README, source listing, assembly and makefiles contain no explicit AI-development disclosure. AI usage remains unknown.

relationships.note: Both demo outputs belong to the same original-author archive. The README credits the Atari toolkit Docker/VASM environment for rebuilding; the archive is distinct from the author's separately tracked modern silly demo and MIDI Maze project.

identity.note: The repository name is le-mans-minigame, but its current upstream title is FASTER. Jonathan Thomas/Chicane describes a from-scratch 2.5D racing game for Atari STE. The source tree contains game loop, car/opponent logic, collision detection, road rendering, audio code and asset generators.

classification.note: This is substantial native homebrew with its own gameplay and rendering implementation. No original game binary is claimed as its source, so source platforms/CPU and reverse-engineering work kinds are left empty; the repository root identifies the coherent game.

source_cpu.note: FASTER is described as built from the ground up for STE rather than a reconstruction of a historical binary. There is no demonstrated original binary CPU to assign.

target_cpu.note: The Makefile uses m68k-atarimegabrowner-elf-gcc with -D__M68000__ and -m68000, and assembles platform routines using vasmm68k_mot. This directly establishes a native 68000 output target.

build.note: README confirms that the Makefile works on macOS and documents its required specific bigbrownbuild GCC, VASM, VLINK and asset/disk tools. It describes the playable racing game and how to run the generated lemans.st on STE hardware or Hatari, supporting author-reported compilable/runnable/playable values. Limitations: The release directory currently contains only .gitkeep; this is not a claim that a ready disk image is bundled there. relationships.note: The project credits Dma-sc music, Junosix mixer enhancement, Zerkman YM playback and Masteries original PCM mixer. It is its own native racing game, distinct from the same author's already tracked Lotus, RoadBlasters and Stunt Car Racer patch projects.

identity.note: Mårten Rånge/Lance preserves the third version of his 1993 STE replay system and explains its history and implementation in a detailed first-person README. PT_SRC50.S contains the replay/Paula emulation implementation, PT_INFO.S documents use and compatibility, and REPLAY.S/REPLAY50.S provide integration examples.

classification.note: This is a substantive original-source music-development library/archive: it combines a ProTracker replay routine with native STE Paula emulation and self-generating mixer code. The historical source and retrospective explain earlier reverse-engineering lineage, but the current archive is not mislabelled as a new binary-derived reconstruction. Its emulator classification concerns sound-chip behavior, not a game-specific guest-CPU wrapper.

source_cpu.note: The preserved historical STE implementation uses 68000 registers and instructions, supervisor/user switching and Atari hardware access; the author explicitly discusses 68k instruction timing and its 8 MHz STE implementation. The record describes this preserved ST-family source rather than treating the use of Amiga music formats as proof of an analyzed Amiga binary.

target_cpu.note: PT_SRC50.S and REPLAY.S directly implement the native 68000 replay routine and STE DMA/LCM1992 output path. There is no portable host or alternate CPU output established by this archive.

build.note: The archive contains complete substantial assembly and example integration sources, with the author documenting its historical release and later use. A present-day build/run is not established: PT_SRC50.S expects an external modules\*.mod input, and the examples use period-style include paths with no modern build automation. Limitations: Current compilability, runnable output and byte equivalence stay unknown. Historical success and author performance estimates are not independent tests of the archived checkout.

runtime_profiles.note: PT_INFO.S explicitly targets STE and warns that this original version is not Falcon-compatible because of stack techniques and the missing LCM1992. Neither it nor the reviewed source establishes a complete minimum-memory runnable configuration, so no minimum runtime profile is inferred.

ai.note: The author history and inspected original-source files contain no explicit AI-development disclosure. The age of the original code does not justify asserting non-use across the repository's later history.

relationships.note: The author explains an early derivation from a recovered Dr. Doom STE replay routine and use of a lightly patched ProTracker player, with the Paula emulator rewritten for version 3. README points to later bug fixes by Mrs Beanbag/RiFT, Paulo Simoes and SMFX; their changes are not attributed to this preserved original version, and the lost UCDM plugin source is not claimed to be present.

identity.note: Claus Schlereth's repository reconstructs the Hagensoft 1.05 and 1.21 add-on ROMs for COMAL80 Revision 2.01, with shared and revision-specific assembly.

ai.note: The reviewed README, source headers and repository tree contain no explicit AI-development disclosure. Non-use is not established.

identity.note: Mark Seelye's ScottFree64/128 ports Alan Cox's DOS ScottFree 1.14b C interpreter. The inspected source includes a native game loop, Commodore I/O, assembly parsing and C128 banked-memory support.

relationships.note: The repository credits Alan Cox's ScottFree source, ScottKit definition corrections and a shortened cc65 C128 memory driver. Bundled third-party adventure data is convenience content, not separate reconstruction work by this author.

identity.note: Dissector is fieserWolF's 6502 disassembler, with Streetuff's optional GUI. The implementation decodes binary input using opcode/addressing-mode tables and emits assembly with C64 labels.

ai.note: The reviewed README, implementation header and root listing provide no explicit development-AI disclosure; absence does not establish non-use.

identity.note: Amiga Game Kit is a coherent root-scoped toolkit plus demonstration games, native debug runtime, test scenarios and asset pipelines. The reviewed README, template, build script and profile implementation agree on that scope.

classification.note: Modern retro-development tooling integrates native C/ACE compilation, reproducible joystick/frame scenarios, golden-image checks, serial state capture and game-asset conversion.
